title: California SB 868 Signed: Plug-In Solar Legal Starting 2027
dek: SB 868 lets Californians use plug-in solar up to 1,200 watts without a utility interconnection agreement starting January 1, 2027.
keyPoints: Governor Newsom signed SB 868, by Senator Scott Wiener, on September 30, 2026; it takes effect January 1, 2027.
Systems are capped at 1,200 watts AC per dwelling and must be certified by UL or an equivalent lab.
Qualifying devices are exempt from utility interconnection agreements; utilities may ask for free online registration.
The interconnection exemption sunsets January 1, 2030, unless lawmakers extend it.

sources.title: Newsom signs California plug-in solar bill, establishing the nation's largest balcony solar market - pv magazine USA
Bill Status - SB-868 Electricity: portable solar generation devices.
California Legalizes Plug-In Solar: Newsom Signs SB 868

body: Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 868, the Plug Into the Sun Act by Senator Scott Wiener, on September 30, 2026. The law takes effect January 1, 2027, and allows portable solar devices that plug into a standard household outlet, often called balcony solar.

What the law does. A qualifying system is capped at 1,200 watts of AC output for a single dwelling and must be certified by UL or an equivalent testing laboratory. Qualifying devices are exempt from utility interconnection requirements, and utilities cannot require permission or charge fees for installing or using them. According to Solar.com, utilities may ask owners to register the device through a free online form. The Assembly Appropriations Committee added a sunset, so the interconnection exemption ends January 1, 2030, unless the Legislature extends it.

Who supported it. Backers included the Environmental Working Group, the California Solar and Storage Association, the Sierra Club and the nonprofit Bright Saver. California joins nine other states that had already passed plug-in solar laws, according to pv magazine.

What it means for contractors. These kits are designed as do-it-yourself products, so they will not replace permitted rooftop systems. They may still reach your business. Renters and condo owners who cannot install rooftop solar are the most likely buyers, and some will ask electricians whether their outlets and circuits can handle one. Solar.com reports that no kit on the market yet met every requirement of the bill at signing, with compliant products expected around spring 2027.
Step 1: Brief your sales and office staff so they can explain the difference between a 1,200-watt plug-in kit and a permitted rooftop system with storage.
Step 2: Electrical contractors may want a standard service call for checking a customer's receptacle and circuit before they plug in a kit.
Step 3: Watch for guidance from your utilities on registration and from local building departments on any safety expectations.
Today's next step: read the bill text and status on the official leginfo page so your team can answer customer questions accurately.
